title: Don't be turned into a Caesar
word: Don't be turned into a Caesar
hook: beware of becoming an emperor inside; stay simple, kind, unaffected (Meditations 6.30)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus called his purple robe sheep's wool dyed in shellfish blood. Your line was wool and shellfish. What did you describe plainly? Day two hundred.

Day two hundred. Look how far you've walked. Now, think of someone who got promoted and changed. Not overnight. Just a little at a time. They started saying we at the leadership level. They stopped eating lunch with the old team. Their jokes got less funny and everyone laughed harder. It happens to people with a little power everywhere: the team lead, the head of the committee, the person with a few thousand followers. Marcus had all the power there was. And he watched himself for exactly this. Today: don't be turned into a Caesar.
screen: `DAY TWO HUNDRED.` → `A LITTLE AT A TIME.` → `DON'T BE TURNED INTO A CAESAR.`

segments.voice: Here's how Book Six, section thirty, begins in George Long's translation: "Take care that thou art not made into a Cæsar, that thou art not dyed with this dye." And then three small words: for such things happen. Remember the dye from a week ago? The soul is dyed by the thoughts. Here Marcus fears a particular color, the color of being emperor, soaking in until it's all the way through. In Greek he uses what looks like a word he invented, something like: don't get Caesared. Being called Caesar was his job. He's afraid of Caesar becoming who he is. So what's the cure? He makes a list for himself: stay simple, good, pure, serious, free from showing off, a friend of justice, reverent toward the gods, kind, affectionate, and strong in doing what's right. And then he does something moving. He holds up a picture of the man who raised him to the throne, his adoptive father, the emperor Antoninus Pius. Marcus remembers how steady he was, how gentle, how little he cared for empty fame, how carefully he listened, how he never rushed a decision. How he was content with plain food and a plain bed. Marcus is telling himself: be his pupil still. Life is short, he adds. The only fruit of this life is a good character and acts that help others. You probably aren't about to be made an emperor. But everyone gets some little throne: a title, a role, a bit of being needed. The question is whether it stays a job or becomes a costume you can't take off. Your line: stay simple.
screen: `TAKE CARE: NOT MADE INTO A CAESAR.` · `A LIST: SIMPLE, GOOD, KIND.` · `REMEMBER ANTONINUS.` · then, large: `STAY SIMPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one bit of status. Settle, and notice which little throne you sit on. A title, being the one who knows, being the busy one, being the one people come to. Now imagine setting it on the floor for these two minutes. Underneath it, who's here? Just a person breathing. Rest as that person. The bell holds the time.
Don't be turned into a Caesar. Marcus warned himself not to let being emperor dye him through, and to stay simple, good and kind. Today's word.
screen: `DON'T BE TURNED INTO A CAESAR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: stay simple. Today, do one thing your role would normally excuse you from: clear the table, answer the phone, take the smaller chair. Day two hundred.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use this passage as a check on their own roles and titles, and many traditions have practices of humility for people in positions of power.

original.note: Greek: from Marcus's warning 'don't be Caesared', a word that appears to be his own coinage.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't become a tyrant.
what it means: don't let your role soak into you until it's who you are.
what a scholar hears: an apparent coinage, apokaisarōthēs, 'be un-made into a Caesar', beside baphēs, 'be dyed', echoing the dye image of 5.16.

sources.quoted: Take care that thou art not made into a Cæsar, that thou art not dyed with this dye

notes: Confirm the Long 1862 wording exactly: 'Take care that thou art not made into a Cæsar, that thou art not dyed with this dye; for such things happen.'
Greek 'μὴ ἀποκαισαρωθῇς, μὴ βαφῇς': confirm spelling and accents, and the claim that it appears to be a coinage (commentators generally say so).

The list is paraphrased from Long ('simple, good, pure, serious, free from affectation, a friend of justice, a worshipper of the gods, kind, affectionate, strenuous in all proper acts'). 'Reverent toward the gods' renders 'worshipper of the gods'. Confirm.
Antoninus portrait details (plain food, plain bed, careful listening, no rushing) are paraphrased from 6.30 and 1.16; confirm which are in 6.30.
'The only fruit of this life is a good character and acts that help others' paraphrases 6.30's 'there is only one fruit of this terrene life...'. Confirm.
